analogy.p: Think of the program as a person at a desk and the file as a notebook in a filing cabinet drawer. **Opening** the file is taking the notebook out of the drawer and opening it at the first page. **readLine** reads the next line from the page, and a bookmark (the pointer) moves down one line each time. **writeLine** writes a new line in the notebook. **endOfFile** is noticing there are no more written lines, and **close** is shutting the notebook, saving what you wrote and putting it back so someone else can use it. The analogy breaks down because a person can flip back to any page, whereas a program using readLine can only move forward through the lines in order unless it closes and reopens the file.
analogy.t: A file as a notebook in a drawer

bullets: A **file** is a named collection of data stored on secondary storage. In J277 the files used are **text files**, which store characters.
RAM is volatile and variables are lost at the end of the run; files are **persistent** so the data survives and can be reused next time.
Typical uses in exam questions: saving a high-score table, reading a list of names, storing login details, keeping a stock list, writing a log of events.
A program can **read input from a file** instead of the keyboard, which is useful when there is a lot of data or when the data must be reused without retyping it.
A program can **write output to a file** instead of the screen, so results can be saved, printed or loaded by another program.
Link to other topics: secondary storage (1.2), arrays (2.2) for holding file data in memory, validation (2.3) and databases/SQL (2.2) for larger structured data.
core.p: A variable only lives in **RAM**, which is **volatile**: when the program ends or the computer is switched off, every value is lost. Many real programs must remember things between runs, such as high scores, a list of customers, settings or a log of events. To keep data permanently a program has to store it in a **file** on **secondary storage** (a hard disk, SSD or USB stick), which is **non-volatile**. **File handling** is the set of operations a program uses to open a file, read data from it, write data to it and close it again. The J277 specification expects you to use these basic operations: open, read, write and close.

bullets: A **line** is one row of text in the file; **readLine** and **writeLine** work on one whole line at a time.
A **record** is all the data about one item (one student, one product); a **field** is one piece of data within the record.
In a CSV file the fields in a record are separated by commas, and each record sits on its own line.
Everything read from a text file arrives as a **string**, even if it looks like a number, so numbers must be converted with the casting functions (see data types).
The file name is a string including its extension, for example "scores.txt". If the file is in a different folder you must give the path as well.
Text files are simple and can be opened in any editor, but they have no built-in structure, so searching them means reading line by line.
core.p: A **text file** holds characters, usually split into **lines**. Each line ends with a hidden **end-of-line** (newline) marker that you do not normally see. In exam questions the simplest file layout is one item per line, for example one name per line. Sometimes one line is a whole **record**, meaning all the data about one thing, with the **fields** separated by a comma, such as Ann,16,Leeds. A file made this way is often called a **comma separated values (CSV)** file. The program reads a line as one string and then splits it up if it needs the separate fields.

bullets: Reference language: **myFile = open("sample.txt")**. Every later operation is written as myFile.something, using the file variable.
The file name is a **string**, so it needs speech marks, whereas the file variable does not.
Opening a file for reading starts at the **first line**; the pointer begins at the start of the file.
Python equivalent: myFile = open("sample.txt", "r"). The second item is the **mode**: "r" read, "w" write (replaces everything), "a" append (adds to the end).
The file variable is a name you choose (myFile, f, scoreFile); the exam rewards a sensible, consistent name.
Open the file **once**, outside any loop, then read or write inside the loop. Opening it again inside a loop would restart from the first line each time.
core.p: Before a program can read or write a file it must **open** it. Opening creates a link between the program and the file on disk and prepares the file for use. In the OCR reference language this is written myFile = open("scores.txt"). The value on the right is the file name as a string; the variable on the left (here myFile) is the **file handle** (the name you use for the file in your program from then on). If you try to open a file that does not exist for reading, the program cannot continue normally, so exam answers assume the file is there unless the question says otherwise.

bullets: Reference language: **x = myFile.readLine()** stores the next line in x.
Each call returns the **next unread line** and advances the pointer; you cannot go back unless you close and reopen the file.
The value is a **string**. To add up numbers read from a file use int() or float() on each line: total = total + int(myFile.readLine()).
Python equivalent: line = myFile.readline(). Python may keep the newline character at the end, which is removed with line.strip().
If you only need the first line, one readLine is enough; you do not need a loop.
Reading past the last line is an error in the reference language, so a loop should test for the end of the file first.
core.h: Reading from a file with readLine
core.p: Once the file is open, **readLine** reads **one line** from it and returns that line as a string. The file keeps an invisible **pointer** (position marker) showing which line is next. The first readLine returns the first line and moves the pointer to the second line; the next readLine returns the second line, and so on. This is why reading the whole file needs a loop, and why you must call readLine only once per pass of the loop: calling it twice would skip a line. The returned value is normally stored in a variable or used straight away, for example line = myFile.readLine().

bullets: Reference language: **myFile.endOfFile()** returns a Boolean (True or False).
Standard pattern: **while NOT myFile.endOfFile()** ... **endwhile**.
Inside the loop read exactly one line, then process it, then go round again.
A `for` loop is only suitable if the number of lines is known in advance (for example 10 lines); `while NOT endOfFile` works for any size.
If the file is empty, endOfFile is True straight away, so the loop body never runs. This is correct behaviour, not an error.
Python has no endOfFile; a for loop over the file (for line in myFile) or a while loop testing for an empty string does the same job.
core.h: Detecting the end of the file: endOfFile
core.p: You often do not know how many lines a file contains. The reference language gives the operation **endOfFile()**, which returns **True** when there are no more lines to read and **False** while data remains. It is used as the condition of a **while** loop so that the loop repeats until every line has been processed: while NOT myFile.endOfFile(). The word NOT is needed because we want to keep looping while the end has not yet been reached. Using endOfFile makes the program work however long the file is, which is better than hard-coding a number of lines.

bullets: Reference language pattern: **newFile("example.txt")**, then **myFile = open("example.txt")**, then **myFile.writeLine("Hello World")**, then **myFile.close()**.
**writeLine** writes the text followed by a new line, so the next writeLine starts on a fresh line.
To write a number use str(): myFile.writeLine(str(score)). To write several fields on one line, join them with concatenation and commas: name + "," + str(score).
Python equivalent: myFile = open("example.txt", "w") then myFile.write("Hello World\n"). The \n adds the new line yourself.
Python mode "w" **overwrites** the whole file; mode "a" **appends** to the end and keeps the old data. Choose "a" for a log or a growing high-score list.
Writing happens in a loop when many items are saved: for example loop through an array and writeLine each element.
core.p: To save data a program writes lines to a file. In the OCR reference language a new file is created with **newFile("name.txt")**, then opened, and **writeLine** places one line of text in it: myFile.writeLine("Hello World"). Each writeLine adds a complete line, ending with an end-of-line marker, so repeated writeLine calls produce one item per line. Writing is how a program stores results permanently. Remember that data to be written must be a string, so a number is converted first with str().

bullets: Reference language: **myFile.close()**.
Closing **saves any buffered data** to the disk, so the written lines are not lost.
Closing **frees the file** so it can be opened by another program or by another part of the same program, and frees resources.
Closing prevents **corruption** or a locked file if the program stops later.
Always close **after** the loop, not inside it; closing inside the loop would stop the next readLine working.
Exam tip: if the question asks for the purpose of closing a file, say it saves the data and makes the file available to other programs.
core.p: When the program has finished with a file it must **close** it using myFile.close(). Closing makes sure that any data still waiting in a temporary store (a **buffer**) is actually saved to the disk, and it releases the file so that other programs can use it. If you forget to close a file that has been written to, some data may never be saved or the file may be damaged or locked. Closing is therefore the last step of every file operation, and a mark in almost every file-handling question is for including it.

bullets: **Read all and print**: open; while NOT endOfFile; print(readLine()); endwhile; close.
**Read and total**: set total = 0 before the loop; add int(readLine()) inside the loop; print the total after the loop; close.
**Read and search**: read each line into a variable, compare with the target using ==, and set a found flag or print when it matches.
**Write user input**: ask with input(), then newFile, open, writeLine, close.
**Copy data into an array**: use a counter i, store each line as names[i] = myFile.readLine() and add 1 to i each time.
**Read then write**: read a line, process it (for example convert to upper case), and write the result to a second file; the two files need different file variables.
core.h: The standard patterns you must be able to write
core.p: Almost every file question is one of three patterns, and examiners award marks for each key line. To **read and display** a file you open it, loop with NOT endOfFile, readLine and print inside the loop, then close it. To **read and process** it (total, count, find) you do the same but update a variable inside the loop. To **write** you create or open the file, writeLine the data (often inside a loop), then close. Learning these three skeletons by heart lets you adapt them to any scenario in the exam.

bullets: A line such as **Ann,16,Leeds** contains three fields separated by commas.
**Python: fields = line.split(",")** gives fields[0] = Ann, fields[1] = 16, fields[2] = Leeds (still strings).
Convert numbers: **age = int(fields[1])** before comparing age >= 16 or adding ages.
Comparing strings gives alphabetical (character code) order, so "9" is greater than "10" as text; convert first to compare numerically.
To write a record, join the fields back together: line = name + "," + str(age) + "," + town.
Choosing a delimiter that cannot appear in the data (a comma in an address would break a CSV file) avoids splitting errors.
core.p: When each line is a record such as Ann,16,Leeds, the whole line arrives as one string and has to be split into its fields. In Python this is done with line.split(","), which returns the fields as a list. In reference-language questions you may be shown the fields already separated or asked to describe splitting using the string handling operations (find the position of the comma, then use substring). Every field is still a string, so numerical fields must be converted before they are used in calculations or comparisons, otherwise the comparison compares text, not numbers.

bullets: Write the file lines under each other and put an arrow at line 1: the pointer starts at the first line.
Every call of readLine returns the line at the arrow, then the arrow moves down; count the calls, not the loop passes.
Make a trace table with a column for each variable and a row for each loop pass; do not skip rows.
If total is built with int(), the values are added (12 + 15 = 27); without int() they are joined as text ("12" + "15" = "1215") or cause an error.
The loop stops when endOfFile becomes True, which is after the last line has been read, so the last line **is** processed.
State the final output exactly, including the order and any text before the number.
core.p: Trace questions give you the contents of a file and some code and ask what is output or what is stored. The method is to write the file lines in a list, number them, and track a **pointer** that moves down one line each time readLine is called. Keep a small table for the variables (for example total and line) and update it each loop. Because readLine advances the pointer, two readLine calls in a single pass of the loop read two different lines, a favourite trap in the exam. Check carefully whether the code converts to integers, or concatenates strings.

bullets: Reading past the end of the file causes an error; **endOfFile** prevents it.
Opening a file that does not exist for reading will fail; a robust program checks or handles this case.
Check the values read: a **range check** or **type check** stops text being treated as a number.
An empty file gives an empty or zero result; test for this if the average divides by the number of lines (dividing by zero is an error).
Keep a **backup** or write to a new file so a mistake does not destroy the original data.
Write comments and meaningful names so a reader can follow the file handling steps; this is part of a **robust and maintainable** program.
core.p: Real programs must cope when something goes wrong. A file might not exist, might be empty or might hold data in the wrong format. Good programs check before they read: they use endOfFile so they never read past the end, they validate each value (for example checking that a number is in a sensible range) and they close the file even when the data is bad. In Python an error such as a missing file can be handled with try and except so the program prints a friendly message instead of crashing. J277 does not require exception handling, but you may describe the idea of checking that a file exists and handling errors.

bullets: Arrays and variables: fast and easy but the data is **lost** when the program ends.
Text files: **permanent**, simple, can be created and edited with a text editor, but searching is by reading line by line and there is no structure checking.
Databases (SQL): suited to **large, linked** data; faster searching and more control, but more complex to set up.
Use a file when the amount of data is small or medium, the structure is simple, and it must survive between runs.
Use an array to hold the data **while the program runs** and a file to store it **between runs**: read the file into an array at the start and write the array back at the end.
Link to other topics: records and SQL (2.2), arrays (2.2), data types and casting (2.2), secondary storage (1.2).
core.h: Files compared with other ways of storing data
core.p: A text file is the simplest way to keep data, but it is not the only way. A **variable** or **array** is fast but temporary. A **text file** is permanent and easy to create but can only be searched by reading line by line, so it is slow for large amounts of data and it has no rules to stop bad data. A **database** stores data in tables of records and fields, can be searched quickly with **SQL**, and can prevent duplicate or invalid data. Exam questions on this topic ask you to justify using a file in a particular scenario or to compare it with the alternatives.

exam: **State/Give** (1-2 marks): short answers such as 'to save the data permanently' or 'to make sure all data is written to the disk'. Write the purpose, not a description of the code.
**Explain why a file is used** (2 marks): data in variables is held in RAM and lost when the program ends (1); a file in secondary storage keeps it so it can be used again next time (1).

**Write/Complete a program** (3 to 5 marks): marks are usually for opening the file, a correct loop condition, one readLine (or writeLine) inside the loop, using or printing the value, and closing the file. Include every one.
**Reference language**: use open, readLine, writeLine, endOfFile, close and newFile exactly as the OCR guide shows. Python is also accepted, but keep to one language in an answer.
**Trace** (3 to 4 marks): write the file lines, move a pointer, keep a table. Remember readLine moves the pointer each time it is called.
**Complete the missing line** questions: read the lines above and below; the missing line is often the readLine, the endOfFile condition or the close.
**Describe/compare files and databases** (4 marks): make two contrasted points with a reason for each, for example permanence and searching.
**Algorithm questions**: if the question says the file has a known number of lines use a `for`; otherwise use while NOT endOfFile.
Use sensible variable names and indent the body of the loop; the 6-mark program questions assess readable, logical code as well as correctness.
Check the output wording: if the program writes text with the number (e.g. "Total: " + str(total)) your answer must show both.

mistakes.r: myFile.close() must appear after the processing, to save the data and free the file; it is usually a mark.
mistakes.w: Forgetting to close the file at the end.

mistakes.r: The file name is a string so it needs speech marks: open("scores.txt").
mistakes.w: Writing the file name without speech marks, e.g. open(scores.txt).

mistakes.r: Use while NOT myFile.endOfFile() so the loop works for any length of file.
mistakes.w: Using a `for` loop when the number of lines is not known.

mistakes.r: Each readLine moves to the next line, so a second call skips a line; read once, store it, and use the stored value.
mistakes.w: Calling readLine twice in one loop pass when only one line is wanted.

mistakes.r: Everything read is a string; convert with int() or float() before calculating.
mistakes.w: Treating data read from a file as a number and adding it directly.

mistakes.r: Open once before the loop and close once after it, otherwise the pointer returns to the start.
mistakes.w: Opening the file inside the loop.

mistakes.r: The reason is persistence: the data is kept after the program ends; RAM and variables are lost.
mistakes.w: Saying a file is used because it is 'faster' than an array.

mistakes.r: "w" overwrites the entire file; use append ("a") to add to the end.
mistakes.w: Writing with "w" mode when old data must be kept.

mistakes.r: Without NOT the loop would stop immediately or run when there is nothing to read.
mistakes.w: Forgetting NOT in while NOT myFile.endOfFile().

summary: OCR J277 spec section 2.2 expects you to use basic file handling to open a text file, read data from it with readLine, write data to it with writeLine and close it again, using endOfFile to control loops. It matters because programs need to keep data after they stop running, and file questions in Paper 2 are worth several marks each.

terms.d: A named collection of data stored on secondary storage, so that it persists when the program ends.
A file that stores data as characters, usually organised in lines.
The variable used to refer to an open file in the program, such as myFile.
The operation that links the program to a file so it can be read from or written to.
The operation that reads one line from an open file and returns it as a string, then moves the pointer to the next line.
The operation that writes a line of text, followed by an end-of-line marker, to an open file.
The operation that returns True when there are no more lines to read from the file, otherwise False.
The operation that saves any buffered data, ends the link with the file and makes it available to other programs.
The reference-language operation that creates a new empty file with a given name.
Storage that keeps data when the power is off, such as a hard disk or SSD; also called non-volatile.
All the data about one item or person, stored together, such as one line in a file.
A single piece of data within a record, such as a name or an age.
A text file format in which the fields of a record are separated by commas and each record is on its own line.
A temporary storage area in memory where data waits before it is written to or after it is read from a file.
To add new data to the end of an existing file without removing the data already there.
The invisible marker showing which line of the file will be read next.

worked.ans:
myFile = open("names.txt")
while NOT myFile.endOfFile()
    print(myFile.readLine())
endwhile
myFile.close()
worked.q: The file names.txt holds one name per line. Write a program that displays every name in the file. [4 marks]
steps: Open the file and store it in a file variable: myFile = open("names.txt") (1 mark).
Loop until the end: while NOT myFile.endOfFile() (1 mark).
Inside the loop read one line and display it: print(myFile.readLine()) (1 mark).
End the loop with endwhile, then close the file: myFile.close() (1 mark).

worked.q:
scores.txt contains three lines: 12, 15 and 9. Give the output of this program. [3 marks]
total = 0
myFile = open("scores.txt")
while NOT myFile.endOfFile()
    total = total + int(myFile.readLine())
endwhile
myFile.close()
print(total)
steps: Pass 1: readLine returns "12", int gives 12, total = 0 + 12 = 12.
The end of file is now reached, so the loop stops and 36 is printed.

name = input("Enter your name")
newFile("log.txt")
myFile = open("log.txt")
myFile.writeLine(name)
myFile.close()
Closing the file makes sure the data is actually saved to the disk and releases the file so that other programs can open it.
worked.q: Write a program that asks the user for their name and saves it to a new file called log.txt. Explain why the file must be closed. [5 marks]
steps: Input: name = input("Enter your name") (1 mark).
Write the name and close: myFile.writeLine(name) then myFile.close() (1 mark).
Reason: closing saves any data held in the buffer to the disk and frees the file for other programs (1 mark).
